It is becoming f*cking dangerous: AI agents from Claude Code transformed an ordinary academic reading list into an interactive research lab right inside the browser

Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, gave a dozen agents a stack of 64 research papers with a strict assignment: design a web platform where any user can independently reproduce physical experiments

There you can select a fluid flow model, adjust external conditions, and analyze in real time how the physics of the process changes

The interface allows switching between algorithms right during the scene, inspecting the formulas involved, source scripts, and numerical metrics alongside the graphics

Each link in the team received a clear scope of work:

> rightarrow analysts pull the math, baseline assumptions, and test settings from the texts
> rightarrow coders translate formulas into working algorithms
> rightarrow auditors check the resulting dynamics against the original papers
> rightarrow interface specialists build control panels for every experiment

The danger lies in the fact that a pretty visualization can easily turn out to be mathematically wrong

Therefore, controllers strictly check adherence to mass conservation laws, calculation stability, and accurate matching with the source metrics before launching into production

For every experiment, the interface displays:

the statement being tested
the constants involved
the deviation from the baseline calculation
blind spots requiring additional verification

The resulting sandbox combined 11 approaches and 28 reference scenes. Seven of them matched the original within allowable tolerances, while four remained stuck in "pending revision" status

If you want to run something similar, upload your stack of PDFs into Claude Code and give this command:

Turn these papers into an interactive web complex:

1. Extract working algorithms, mathematical models, and test parameters. Be sure to specify page numbers and highlight gaps
2. Assign different methodologies to isolated agents, unifying them with a shared input field and single measurement tools for correct analytics
3. Set up an independent review stage: let reviewers record bugs, and leave all unverified results clearly marked with warning tags
4. Design convenient controls to tweak parameters, compare methodologies, and run through the source code

It is wiser to start with a single document and a single baseline experiment, gradually scaling up the number of agents

Be sure to pack dependencies and clean input data so that an outside researcher can bring up the entire testbed from scratch with a single button

Full instructions on how to create this can be found in the article below

How to Build a Memory System for Opus 5.5 That Survives Across Sessions: Write, Consolidate, Recall

Every Opus 5.5 session starts from zero.
You spent an hour yesterday explaining your stack, your naming conventions, the client who hates bullet points, the reason you moved off Heroku. Today it's all gone. You explain it again. Tomorrow you'll explain it again.
The model isn't the problem. Opus 5.5 is excellent at using context. The problem is that nothing carries the context from one session to the next.
Most people try to fix this by pasting a giant "about me" document into every chat, or by stuffing old transcripts back into the prompt. Both break fast. The document goes stale. The transcripts get expensive, and they're full of noise: dead ends, bugs you already fixed, opinions you changed.
A real memory system is different. It has four jobs:
Write: after a session, save only the facts worth keeping. Consolidate: every so often, merge, correct and shrink what's saved. Recall: at the start of a request, load the right memories and nothing else. Apply: use a memory only when it actually changes the answer.
This article builds all four from scratch with Opus 5.5, plain files and about 200 lines of Python. Every prompt is copyable. Every piece of code runs.

Anthropic’s model found a molecular shape sitting in public data for forty years that nobody had bothered to name

It was not hidden. It appears across thousands of deposited structures, in proteins that share no function and no ancestry.

> SWEEP - every deposited structure read as geometry, with the biology labels stripped off
> FORM - recurring three dimensional arrangements grouped purely by shape
> CHECK - each group tested against the known motif catalogue to filter out the obvious
> ORPHAN - the shapes that match no catalogued motif kept instead of discarded
> WHERE - each orphan mapped onto what surrounds it in every protein it appears in

Structural biology names motifs the way it finds them: one protein at a time, by someone who noticed.

A shape that spans unrelated families gets missed. Each specialist sees it once and files it as a quirk of their own protein.

Read without labels, the repetition is obvious. The same arrangement, hundreds of times, across proteins that do nothing alike.

Where it sits is the interesting part. It keeps showing up at boundaries, right where one part of a protein hands off to another.

That suggests it is doing something structural rather than chemical. Not a function, but a joint.

Nothing is proven here. It is a named shape and a list of where to look, which is how every motif started.

Public data has been scanned for sequences for decades. Almost nobody scans it for shapes nobody asked about.

The shape, every family it appears in and the boundary pattern are laid out underneath.

Agent takes one paragraph and does the rest alone: opens a terminal, drives Blender, and hands back a film-ready set

Nothing is exported and passed around. It runs Blender headless, writes its own scripts, and iterates until the scene survives a camera.

> SPAWN - the agent opens a shell, launches Blender and works through its API directly
> TEMPLATE - the structures it keeps rebuilding get saved as reusable node setups
> SHOOT - cameras placed on real lens values, so blocking is checked before anyone builds

Concept art answers what a place looks like. It never answers whether two actors and a dolly fit down the hallway.

Every wall, prop and floor arrives on its own layer. A wall that lifts out is a wall the crew can put a camera behind.

The templates compound. The second set costs a fraction of the first, because the agent stopped solving the same problem twice.

Lens values matter more than resolution. A 35mm pass tells you if the geometry works; a beauty render tells you nothing.

Previs normally costs weeks and a small team, which is why most productions skip it and find the problems on the build.

Here it lands before the budget meeting, set standing and blocking already walked through.

The paragraph that started it, the layered file and the full camera pass are laid out underneath.

virals.name: Aakash Gupta
virals.text:
OpenAI just got a problem no better model can fix.

For $8 a month, Elon now sells his AI, an AI coding editor, and X Premium on one bill. Microsoft ran this exact play in 1995 and erased an 80% market leader in four years without ever building the better browser.

The victim was Netscape. It owned the browser market, Microsoft made Internet Explorer free with every copy of Windows, and by 1999 Netscape was selling itself to AOL. Nobody ever found a counter to it.

Today's version is buried in Cursor's reply, where almost nobody will scroll. Paid plans get twice the coding usage on Grok models, and third-party models move to API pricing "to make room for more Grok usage."

Inside the most popular AI coding editor, that means same keystrokes, same tab-complete, one model subsidized by a $1.25 trillion parent while every rival bills at raw list price. Cursor spent three years becoming the biggest storefront for other labs' coding models. SpaceX bought the storefront in August and just repriced everyone else's shelf space.

Look at how fast this came together. February, SpaceX absorbs xAI at a $250 billion valuation. August, it buys Cursor. October, the rename to Superintelligence and one subscription covering the model, the editor, the social network, and your blue check.

Eight months, start to finish.

Bundles win because the extra product feels free. A developer already paying $30 for X plus chat plus coding has to actively talk himself into sending another lab $20 a month on top. Teams passed Slack in daily users within two years of launch for one reason. It rode a bill companies were already paying.

Netscape's browser was better than IE for most of that fight. Ask anyone under 30 if they've ever heard of it.

virals.text:
An OpenAI employee wrapped a recording device in toilet paper and hid it behind the TV in the exec boardroom. OpenAI found it, left the room untouched, and hid a camera behind the same TV. Then they waited for him to come back and check on his bug.

He did.

The guy joined OpenAI's product team in July 2025. Prosecutors say the device was plugged into a USB port on the back of the television, installed about two days before security found it. The room was used by executives, and the FBI director says the goal was capturing conversations about the company's "super intelligence technology."

Here's the detail from the complaint that got me. Prosecutors say he submitted AI prompts about building, customizing, obfuscating, and remote-accessing a continuous audio recorder. He allegedly used AI to engineer the bug he planted inside the world's most famous AI company. And OpenAI says it used its own models to trace the device back to him.

While the FBI built its case, OpenAI quietly restricted his access and put him on leave instead of tipping him off. A second package arrived on October 5. Security opened it and found another recording device. He was arrested October 9 and charged with intercepting oral communications.

This tells you where the real secrets live now. Model weights sit behind some of the heaviest security in tech. Source code is locked down. Customer data gets audited. So the attack went after the one thing nobody can encrypt, which is executives talking out loud in a room.

Frontier labs spent three years hardening servers against nation states. The cheapest way in turned out to be a recorder wrapped in toilet paper, pointed at a room where people speak freely.

Gaming is the single biggest opportunity in AI right now

2027 will be an absolute gold rush for anyone who dedicates the time to build a game with AI

Gaming is BY FAR the biggest entertainment industry on Earth

Double the size of the ENTIRE movie, music, and U.S. sports industry combined (NFL, NBA, NHL, MLB) 

Over the past year the economics of gaming has completely collapsed. Despite the industry making over $200 billion a year, it has become completely unaffordable to make good games anymore

The work needed to make a detailed game that keeps up with today's tech is beyond comprehension

This is where AI comes in. AI fixes those economics

AI allows solo devs to build the AAA games of their dreams with very little resources.

The thing is the gaming industry up to this point has completely rejected AI. This won't last much longer though. Disruption is coming and quite literally nothing is going to stop it

The first domino fell today. Asha the CEO of Xbox announced Xbox Labs today. This appears to be one of the first times a major gaming brand is embracing the disruption (for the record Asha has done an INCREDIBLE job being the shepherd of the Xbox brand)

It is so painfully obvious where all of this is going. In the next 12 months every digital game store will be filled with AAA quality, incredibly fun games built entirely with AI by a single developer

The $200 billion flowing through the gaming industry will be redirected from massive studios with thousands of devs to solo developers/small teams embracing the latest tech

The largest entertainment industry in the world will be 100% owned by indie AI developers. Hundreds of billions of dollars up for grabs

And unlike other sectors of software, gaming has built in moats.

One of the last moats in software will be network effects

If I build a community based piece of software that has a million users and you build the exact same piece of software and it has 0 users, everyone will buy my software instead

Gaming encapsulates this perfectly. If you build a banger multiplayer game that has millions of players, even if someone copies you and builds the exact same game, you're going to win because of network effects

This is one of those moments. One of those moments where the future is so obvious and so clear.

AI is about to disrupt a multi hundred billion dollar industry and every penny of that will be up for grabs.

There is absolutely no reason why you can't be one of the people who capitalizes on this

Download Claude Code. Download Codex. Whatever your choice is, just get it. Then start building the game of your dreams

GTA 6 will be a landmark game for many reasons. One of those reasons is it will be the one of the last AAA games from a massive developer studio. That model doesn't work anymore.

The new model is you. A person with an idea and access to the most powerful technology ever created.

Don't screw this opportunity up.

OpenAI just got a problem no better model can fix.

For $8 a month, Elon now sells his AI, an AI coding editor, and X Premium on one bill. Microsoft ran this exact play in 1995 and erased an 80% market leader in four years without ever building the better browser.

The victim was Netscape. It owned the browser market, Microsoft made Internet Explorer free with every copy of Windows, and by 1999 Netscape was selling itself to AOL. Nobody ever found a counter to it.

Today's version is buried in Cursor's reply, where almost nobody will scroll. Paid plans get twice the coding usage on Grok models, and third-party models move to API pricing "to make room for more Grok usage."

Inside the most popular AI coding editor, that means same keystrokes, same tab-complete, one model subsidized by a $1.25 trillion parent while every rival bills at raw list price. Cursor spent three years becoming the biggest storefront for other labs' coding models. SpaceX bought the storefront in August and just repriced everyone else's shelf space.

Look at how fast this came together. February, SpaceX absorbs xAI at a $250 billion valuation. August, it buys Cursor. October, the rename to Superintelligence and one subscription covering the model, the editor, the social network, and your blue check.

Eight months, start to finish.

Bundles win because the extra product feels free. A developer already paying $30 for X plus chat plus coding has to actively talk himself into sending another lab $20 a month on top. Teams passed Slack in daily users within two years of launch for one reason. It rode a bill companies were already paying.

Netscape's browser was better than IE for most of that fight. Ask anyone under 30 if they've ever heard of it.

An OpenAI employee wrapped a recording device in toilet paper and hid it behind the TV in the exec boardroom. OpenAI found it, left the room untouched, and hid a camera behind the same TV. Then they waited for him to come back and check on his bug.

He did.

The guy joined OpenAI's product team in July 2025. Prosecutors say the device was plugged into a USB port on the back of the television, installed about two days before security found it. Here's the detail from the complaint that got me. Prosecutors say he submitted AI prompts about building, customizing, obfuscating, and remote-accessing a continuous audio recorder. He allegedly used AI to engineer the bug he planted inside the world's most famous AI company. And OpenAI says it used its own models to trace the device back to him.

While the FBI built its case, OpenAI quietly restricted his access and put him on leave instead of tipping him off. A second package arrived on October 5. Security opened it and found another recording device. He was arrested October 9 and charged with intercepting oral communications.

This tells you where the real secrets live now. Model weights sit behind some of the heaviest security in tech. Source code is locked down. Customer data gets audited. So the attack went after the one thing nobody can encrypt, which is executives talking out loud in a room.

Frontier labs spent three years hardening servers against nation states. The cheapest way in turned out to be a recorder wrapped in toilet paper, pointed at a room where people speak freely.

outsiders.name: Alex Finn
outsiders.text:
Gaming is the single biggest opportunity in AI right now

2027 will be an absolute gold rush for anyone who dedicates the time to build a game with AI

Gaming is BY FAR the biggest entertainment industry on Earth

Double the size of the ENTIRE movie, music, and U.S. sports industry combined (NFL, NBA, NHL, MLB) 

Over the past year the economics of gaming has completely collapsed. Despite the industry making over $200 billion a year, it has become completely unaffordable to make good games anymore

The work needed to make a detailed game that keeps up with today's tech is beyond comprehension

This is where AI comes in. AI fixes those economics

AI allows solo devs to build the AAA games of their dreams with very little resources.

The thing is the gaming industry up to this point has completely rejected AI. This won't last much longer though. Disruption is coming and quite literally nothing is going to stop it

The first domino fell today. Asha the CEO of Xbox announced Xbox Labs today. This appears to be one of the first times a major gaming brand is embracing the disruption (for the record Asha has done an INCREDIBLE job being the shepherd of the Xbox brand)

It is so painfully obvious where all of this is going. In the next 12 months every digital game store will be filled with AAA quality, incredibly fun games built entirely with AI by a single developer

The $200 billion flowing through the gaming industry will be redirected from massive studios with thousands of devs to solo developers/small teams embracing the latest tech

The largest entertainment industry in the world will be 100% owned by indie AI developers. Hundreds of billions of dollars up for grabs

And unlike other sectors of software, gaming has built in moats.

One of the last moats in software will be network effects

If I build a community based piece of software that has a million users and you build the exact same piece of software and it has 0 users, everyone will buy my software instead

Gaming encapsulates this perfectly. If you build a banger multiplayer game that has millions of players, even if someone copies you and builds the exact same game, you're going to win because of network effects

This is one of those moments. One of those moments where the future is so obvious and so clear.

AI is about to disrupt a multi hundred billion dollar industry and every penny of that will be up for grabs.

There is absolutely no reason why you can't be one of the people who capitalizes on this

Download Claude Code. Download Codex. Whatever your choice is, just get it. Then start building the game of your dreams

GTA 6 will be a landmark game for many reasons. One of those reasons is it will be the one of the last AAA games from a massive developer studio. That model doesn't work anymore.

The new model is you. A person with an idea and access to the most powerful technology ever created.

Don't screw this opportunity up.
